ling-soc-01-c1.text: J. K. Chambers and Peter Trudgill (1998). Dialectology, Second Edition. Cambridge University Press.
ling-soc-01-c1.quote: we consider Norwegian, Swedish, Danish and German to be single languages for reasons that are as much political, geographical, historical, sociological and cultural as linguistic.
ling-soc-01-c1.claim: Whether two varieties count as dialects or separate languages is often political rather than purely linguistic.

ling-soc-01-c1.text: J. K. Chambers and Peter Trudgill (1998). Dialectology, Second Edition. Cambridge University Press.
ling-soc-01-c1.quote: While it is true, for example, that many Swedes can very readily understand many Norwegians, it is also clear that they often do not understand them so well as they do other Swedes.
ling-soc-01-c1.claim: Norwegian and Swedish are called 'languages' but are mutually intelligible.

ling-soc-01-c2.text: William Labov (1972). The Social Stratification of (r) in New York City Department Stores (chapter in Sociolinguistic Patterns). University of Pennsylvania Press.
ling-soc-01-c2.quote: The three stores which were selected are Saks Fifth Avenue, Macy's, and S. Klein.
ling-soc-01-c2.claim: He visited three department stores of different prestige (Saks Fifth Avenue, Macy's, S. Klein) and asked for items on the fourth floor to elicit the phrase with post-vocalic /r/.
